intro: The Forlane, the third movement of Le Tombeau de Couperin, takes the rhythm of an old dance and sets it to chords that move in unexpected directions. It is dedicated to the memory of Gabriel Deluc, a Basque painter killed in the First World War.

sections.label: B · Detached chords over held notes
sections.mNote: The bass holds while the upper chords move.

sections.label: C · Dotted figures and trills
sections.mNote: Short dance phrases with added ornaments.

sections.label: Coda · Softly, at the same pace
sections.mNote: The closing bars stay in tempo, sans ralentir.

cues.title: Forlane, opening
cues.text: Ravel marks the 6/8 dance Allegretto, and long–short figures set its rhythm. From the quiet opening, the melody moves step by step through chords full of sharps and naturals. The first short strain is repeated.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, opening; Piano Practical Editions, bars 1–16, p. 18. The score has dotted figures, chromatic chord notes and a repeat after bar 8. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Gabriel Deluc
cues.text: This dance is dedicated to Lieutenant Gabriel Deluc. He was a Basque painter and a friend of Ravel, and one of the men killed in the First World War who are commemorated in Le Tombeau de Couperin.
cues.evidence: The BnF records Deluc’s dedication and rank: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. His profession, friendship and death in the war are documented by Eric T. Williams, Kansas City Symphony programme, 5–7 April 2024, p. 6: https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf

cues.title: Ravel’s Couperin transcription
cues.text: Before writing his own Forlane, Ravel transcribed a forlane by François Couperin. The dance came from northern Italy and was taken up at the French court around 1700. Ravel’s movement keeps its dotted step and repeated phrases and sets them to his own chords.
cues.evidence: Eric T. Williams describes Ravel’s Couperin transcription, the dance’s Italian origins and its French courtly history, Kansas City Symphony programme, 5–7 April 2024, pp. 6–7. https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf

cues.title: Chords over a held bass
cues.text: The piano alternates detached chords with notes held across the beat. A bass note can sound on while the upper parts move to the next chord. The two dotted-crotchet beats of 6/8 continue throughout.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, pp. 12–13: detached chordal writing, sustained lower voices and continuing 6/8 metre.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trills and grace notes
cues.text: The later phrases keep the dance’s long–short rhythm and add trills and short grace notes. During a trill on one note, the phrase continues in the other parts. A footnote at the opening of the Durand score (1918) specifies that grace notes fall on the beat.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, pp. 14–15, including the trill in the closing pages; the opening footnote specifies that grace notes fall on the beat.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Final bars, sans ralentir
cues.text: The final gestures are short and widely spaced. Over the last pianissimo chord Ravel writes sans ralentir (without slowing).
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, final bars; Piano Practical Editions, p. 26, preserves the final pp and sans ralentir.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The close, without slowing
transitions.to: Coda · Softly, at the same pace
transitions.how: The piano breaks the dance into short phrases, rests and sustained notes. A last grace-note figure leads to a soft chord over a low E. Ravel marks the ending pianissimo and sans ralentir, and the 6/8 metre continues to the final bar.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, p. 15; Piano Practical Editions, final bars, p. 26.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
